Before we get started, change the YAML to have your name as the author instead of mine.

This week we have explored some of the data wrangling functions in R, focusing specifically on the `{tidyverse}` set of packages. So, first off we need to load the `{tidyverse}` packages. 

```{r}
#| label: load-packages

library(tidyverse)
```

:::{.callout-tip title="💡 Remember 💡" icon=false}
If you get an error such as `"Error: package or namespace load failed for '[name of the package]' in loadNamespace"` this means you do not have the package installed on your computer. You can always check which packages are installed by going to the "Packages" tab in RStudio. If the package is listed, you have it installed. If there is a tick mark by the name, it is loaded and active in your current R session. 
:::

In this practice document we will be using a familiar set of data from Public Health Scotland (Scottish Heart Disease activity and morality by health board) that we have used in previous tutorials in Week 2 and Week 4. Only now, you have the tools to understand all of the wrangling code - how exciting! 🎉

For the example data today, we will return to the [Scottish Heart Disease Statistics from Public Health Scotland](https://www.opendata.nhs.scot/dataset/scottish-heart-disease-statistics). There are 2 datasets we are interested in:

1. [Heart Disease Activity by Health Board]("https://www.opendata.nhs.scot/dataset/0e17f3fc-9429-48aa-b1ba-2b7e55688253/resource/748e2065-b447-4b75-99bd-f17f26f3eaef/download/hd_activitybyhbr.csv")

2. [Health Board look up](https://www.opendata.nhs.scot/dataset/9f942fdb-e59e-44f5-b534-d6e17229cc7b/resource/652ff726-e676-4a20-abda-435b98dd7bdc), which allows us to connect the datasets based on the Health Board codes.

:::{.callout-note title="Navigating the Document"}
Work through the following tasks with your partner, or on your own. There is a sample completed practice document on Learn under Week 5 Tutorial Resources that you can check later for example solutions - remember, there are many different ways of doing the same thing in R! 

If you wrote code that works, and the example solution is different, both may very well be correct. The most important thing is that **you** understand your code and that it runs effectively (doing what you want it to do).

# Wrangling Practice 

## Task 1

Load in the data sets and save them in your working environment. Call them `activity_raw `and `hb`. 

To load in our data, we need the `{tidyverse}` suite of package (specifically `{readr}`) loaded, which we have done in the libraries code chunk at the top. With these data sets, it is quite easy to import the data as we can use the website URLs to access the most recent version of the data. 

The URLs to access the data are

* Activity data: https://www.opendata.nhs.scot/dataset/0e17f3fc-9429-48aa-b1ba-2b7e55688253/resource/748e2065-b447-4b75-99bd-f17f26f3eaef/download/hd_activitybyhbr.csv

* Health Board look-up: https://www.opendata.nhs.scot/dataset/9f942fdb-e59e-44f5-b534-d6e17229cc7b/resource/652ff726-e676-4a20-abda-435b98dd7bdc/download/hb14_hb19.csv

```{r}
#| label: task-1
#| message: false

activity_raw <- read_csv("https://www.opendata.nhs.scot/dataset/0e17f3fc-9429-48aa-b1ba-2b7e55688253/resource/748e2065-b447-4b75-99bd-f17f26f3eaef/download/hd_activitybyhbr.csv")

hb <- read_csv("https://www.opendata.nhs.scot/dataset/9f942fdb-e59e-44f5-b534-d6e17229cc7b/resource/652ff726-e676-4a20-abda-435b98dd7bdc/download/hb14_hb19.csv") 

```


## Task 2

Now that we have our 2 data sets saved to our global environment, use your favourite functions for eyeballing data and write a couple of sentences about each data set (its dimensions, the variables inside, types of data, etc.)

```{r}
#| label: task-2

## Glimpse is useful for a quick overview 
glimpse(activity_raw)

glimpse(hb)

# or the tidyverse piping approach 
hb |>
  glimpse()

## skimr::skim() is great for more detailed information 

skimr::skim(activity_raw)
```


The `activity_raw` data set has 43,200 rows and 15 columns. Of these 15 variables, 9 are characters, 3 are logical, and 3 are numeric. 

The `hb` data set has 18 rows and 5 columns. These 5 columns or variables are largely characters, with 2 numeric or double variable types. 

## Task 3 

Our second data set, `hb`, helps us to identify what the health board codes mean in the `activity_raw` data set. Lets join the `hb` data set to the `activity_raw` data set, calling the new data set `activity_joined`. 

What type of join do you think would be best to use?  

➡️ **Answer**: Here I have chosen to use a **left join** as I want to keep all of the data from `activity_raw` (x) and only the matching data from `hb` (y). 

:::{.callout-tip}
## ❓ Hint 

Now that you have decided on the type of join, have a look at the data frames you want to join and look for the **key** - the variable present in both datasets that they will be joined by. They may not have the same name, but represent the same data 
:::


```{r}
#| label: task-3

activity_joined <- activity_raw |> 
  # join activity to hb 
  left_join(hb, by = join_by(Hbr == HB))

## the above solution is ideal for then further wrangling data in a single workflow/pipeline using the pipe. Another solution without the pipe is below 

activity_joined2 <- left_join(activity_raw, hb, by = join_by(Hbr == HB))

```


## Task 4 

Notice that we now have 43,200 observations or rows in our data (as we did with `activity_raw`). However, now we have 19 variables or columns. Do we need all of these variables if we are interested in the Health Board name, year, admission type, diagnosis, number of discharges, and demographic variables of the patients? I do not think so. 

To check the names of columns in your data object, you can use the `names()` function.

Select only the variables of interest and save this in a new data set called `activity_selected`. 

:::{.callout-caution title="📝 Note" icon="false"}
Remember, we want to use our joined data set we created in Task 3, not the original data set. 
:::

```{r}
#| label: task-4

activity_joined |> 
  names()

activity_selected <- activity_joined |>  
   select(FinancialYear, 
         HBName, 
         AdmissionType,
         AgeGroup,
         Sex,
         Diagnosis,
         NumberOfDischarges)

```


## Task 4.2 

What format is the data currently in? Long or wide? 

➡️ **Answer**: The data is in **long format**. Wide format is where we have a single row for every data point with multiple columns to hold the values of various attributes. Long format is where, for each data point we have as many rows as the number of attributes and each row contains the value of a particular attribute for a given data point.

To explore the dataset shape, I clicked on the data object in the global environment to open the viewer tab and returned to Task 2 functions for eyeballing the data. `names()` is also useful to ensure that the column names do not contain any values. 


## Task 5

Now that we have our variables of interest in our data set, how might we get a summary of the `NumberofDischarges` variable? What about the `AdmissionType` variable? 

Do you notice any differences between the summary information available? Why might this be? 

➡️ **Answer**: 

```{r}
#| label: task-5

activity_selected |>  
  select(NumberOfDischarges) |>  
  summary()

activity_selected |> 
  select(AdmissionType) |>  
  summary()

```

`NumberOfDischarges` is a numeric variable, so we get summary descriptive statistics of the central tendency (like the mean, median) and dispersion of the data (like minimum and maximum values). 

`AdmissionType` is a character variable. We want it to be treated as a categorical variable, or factor. So we need to change the variable type first to get a meaningful summary of the variable. 

## Task 5.2 

Change the `AdmissionType` variable to be a factor and then look at the summary. 

:::{.callout-tip}
## ❓ Hint 

You can use the same answer as above, but need to add a function to change the variable class in the workflow/pipeline 
:::

```{r}
#| label: task-5-2

activity_selected |> 
  mutate(AdmissionType_f = fct(AdmissionType)) |>  
  select(AdmissionType_f) |> 
  summary()

# NOTE: I did not save this data flow into a new data frame object, so I cannot call on AdmissionType_f again elsewhere in my code unless I either include the mutate line again in a new data flow or save it into an new data frame 

# NOTE 2: here either forcats::fct() or factor() would work 

```


## Task 6 

We can see from our result in Task 5.2 that there are aggregate levels of the variable "All" included with the specific levels "Elective", "Emergency", and "Transfer". How might we look look at only the aggregate levels of the variable?

:::{.callout-tip}
## ❓ Hint 

Make sure you check how the different levels of the variable are spelled. R will treat "all" differently from "All" - but you *will not get an error* in this case. Try your code with "all" and "All" to see what I mean. 
:::


```{r}
#| label: task-6

activity_selected |>  
  filter(AdmissionType == "All")

# change to all and see what happens

```


## Task 6.2 

How might we look look at only the non-aggregate levels of the variable `AdmissionType`?

```{r}
#| label: task-6-2

activity_selected |>  
  filter(AdmissionType != "All")

# or you could select only the levels we want to keep, rather than NOT the levels to keep 
activity_selected |> 
  filter(AdmissionType %in% c("Elective", "Emergency", "Transfer"))

# both approaches work and result in a data frame (or tibble - a tidyverse version of a data frame) with 32,400 observations/rows and 7 variables/columns 

```


## Task 6.3 

What if we wanted to remove all of the aggregate levels from all of our variables of interest? 

:::{.callout-tip}
## ❓ Hint 

Go back to Task 5 and Task 5.2 and repeat these steps for the other character variables in our data set `activity_selected`
:::

There are 2 steps to answer this question: identify aggregate rows, filter them out. Below I include a more advanced solution to step 1, see if you can follow how it works! 

```{r}
#| label: task-6-3-step1

# first we need to look at the summary of our variables. But to see this we need to convert the variable class from character to factor 
activity_selected |>  
  mutate(FinancialYear_f = factor(FinancialYear),
         HBName_f = factor(HBName),
         AdmissionType_f = factor(AdmissionType),
         AgeGroup_f = factor(AgeGroup),
         Sex_f = factor(Sex),
         Diagnosis_f = factor(Diagnosis)) |>  
  select(FinancialYear_f,
         HBName_f,
         AdmissionType_f,
         AgeGroup_f,
         Sex_f,
         Diagnosis_f) |> 
  summary()
```

A more advanced solution to step 1 

```{r}
#| label: task-6-3-step1-adv

# a more advanced solution
activity_selected |> 
  # first select only the character columns from the data, not necessary but does make the summary only our variables of interest
  select(where(is.character)) |> 
  # then make all of the character columns into factors using mutate() and across() (to apply the function across multiple columns) and where() (which is a tidy selection helper function)
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor)) |>   
  summary()

## If doing mutate first makes more sense, then the solution would be 
activity_selected |>  
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor)) |> 
  # selecting here factors only since we changed all characters to factors first 
  select(where(is.factor)) |> 
  summary()
```

`AgeGroup` has 2 aggregate variables! Sneaky 

You can also see that we cannot view all of the levels for some of the variables. This is because the print out is too long for `summary()`. You can instead use the `distinct()` function or change the `maxsum` argument in `summary()` to be a higher number, default is 7 which is why any more than 7 levels are cut off from the print out 

```{r}
#| label: task-6-3

# Solution changing summary print out number 
activity_selected |>  
  select(where(is.character)) |> 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor)) |> 
  summary(maxsum = 20)

# Solution using distinct on specific variables 
activity_selected |> 
  distinct(HBName)

```

You can see that we have a sneaky `NA` in `HBName`! 

```{r task6-3-step2}
# We can now filter now that we know what we want to filter out 
activity_selected |> 
  filter(Sex != "All" & 
           AgeGroup != "All" & 
           AgeGroup != "under75 years" &
           AdmissionType != "All" & 
           HBName != "NA")
## NAs produced from S92000003 in the join which is the country code for all of Scotland  

# instead of & you could also use commas
activity_selected |>  
  filter(Sex != "All",
         AgeGroup != "All" , 
         AgeGroup != "under75 years", 
         AdmissionType != "All", 
         HBName != "NA")
```


## Task 7 

As we discussed in the tutorial, `mutate()` and `summarise()` are similar though distinct functions. Change the mutate function below to be summarise instead - what do you expect to see? 

```{r}
#| label: task-7

activity_selected |> 
  mutate(mean_discharge = mean(NumberOfDischarges, na.rm = TRUE)) 

activity_selected |> 
  summarise(mean_discharge = mean(NumberOfDischarges, na.rm = TRUE)) 

```

## Additional note around descriptive statistics 

While there are not any `NA` values in the `NumberOfDischarges` column, it is a good idea to include the `na.rm = TRUE` argument when computing the mean or standard deviation to make your code robust to any data updates (where NAs might appear). This argument is a logical (taking `TRUE` or `FALSE` in response) argument to remove `NA` values in the calculation. If there are missing values when calculating the mean or standard deviation, you will not receive an error but instead your outcome will be an `NA`, even when there is data there and it is an applicable function.

In the code chunk below I have created a simple tibble with some `NA` values so that you can see this in practice. 

```{r}
#| label: mean-with-na

jackolantern_data <- tibble(pumpkins = 1:5,
                            carvings = c(1,2,NA,4,NA),
                            tea_lights = c(NA,2,3,NA,NA))

# lets have a look at the data by printing it 
jackolantern_data

# now lets summarise the toy dataset into the mean of each column 
jackolantern_data |> 
  summarise(mean_pumpkins = mean(pumpkins),
            mean_carvings = mean(carvings),
            mean_tea_lights = mean(tea_lights))
```

The `NA`s have disrupted our calculations for `mean_carvings` and `mean_tea_lights`! But we did not get an error. And we know there are values in some of the rows. Add in the argument to have the `NA`s ignored into the code and run it again. 

## Task 8

Add in the argument to have the `NA`s ignored into the code and run it again. 

If you want to challenge yourself, format the mean values to 1 decimal place for all columns int the summary tibble. 

```{r}
#| label: task-8

jackolantern_data |> 
  summarise(mean_pumpkins = mean(pumpkins, na.rm = TRUE) |> round(1),
            mean_carvings = mean(carvings, na.rm = TRUE) |> round(1),
            mean_tea_lights = mean(tea_lights, na.rm = TRUE) |> round(1))

```


# Benefits and considerations of a tidy workflow 

A very cool aspect of working with the `{tidyverse}` is that you can immediately use a variable you have created through the `mutate()` function without having to save it into an object or data frame. 

For example, in the solution code to Task 5.2, I created a new variable called `AdmissionType_f` and immediately used in the following line of code in the select function.

```{r}
#| label: ex-1
#| eval: false

activity_selected |> 
  mutate(AdmissionType_f = fct(AdmissionType)) |>  
  select(AdmissionType_f) |> 
  summary()
```

This can be super useful when wrangling data for plotting (which we will explore next week), or creating tables. 

One of the things to note is that in a tidy work flow, the code is executed in order. Remember, you can read the `|>` as saying "and then". So the following code in the `ex-2` code chunk in plain language would be "Take the `activity_select` data set and then select the variables `AgeGroup`, `Diagnosis`, and `HBName` and then mutate or change the `HBName` variable to be a factor" 

```{r}
#| label: ex-2
#| eval: false

activity_joined |>  
  select(AgeGroup, Diagnosis, HBName) |> 
  mutate(HBName = factor(HBName))
```

:::{.callout-important}
‼️ This means that **the order of your code matters!**. You must thinking logically about the order in which you are asking R to do things. ‼️
:::

You can only mutate variables which are currently selected - see the error in the code below 

```{r}
#| label: tidyflow-error

#activity_joined |>  
#  select(AgeGroup, Diagnosis) |>  
#  mutate(HBName = factor(HBName))

#I have commented out the code here in order for the file to render. A Quarto document will not render if there are errors in the code. Remove the comments and try and render the file to see what I mean! 
```

The error code here is actually quite helpful `"! object HBName not found"`. This tells us that the `mutate()` function cannot do as we are asking it to do because R cannot find the variable called `HBName`. This is because we have selected only `AgeGroup` and `Diagnosis` from the data set, meaning we can now only work with those variables. 

To solve this error we can (a) add `HBName` to our select function or (b) move the mutate function before the select function. 

That's all for now! :)
